content: Monitoring treatment outcomes, including early detection of treatment failure, is essential for managing drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB). Generating additional evidence on adverse events is critical to building a robust safety profile for new treatment regimens across diverse settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment, particularly for drug-resistant TB, in 2022. Adjustments in the dosing and duration of linezolid, when necessary, are important to inform the evidence base for the broader use of the BPaLM/BPaL regimens and to assess the tolerability of linezolid within these regimens. WHO suggests using a 9-month all-oral regimen instead of longer 18-month regimens for patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) who do not have fluoroquinolone resistance. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty of evidence. The 9-month all-oral regimen includes bedaquiline (used for 6 months) combined with levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and clofazimine for 4 months (extendable to 6 months if the patient remains sputum smear-positive at the end of 4 months). This is followed by 5 months of treatment with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Ethionamide can be replaced with 2 months of linezolid (600 mg daily). The regimen with linezolid instead of ethionamide may be used in pregnant women, unlike the ethionamide-containing regimen. This recommendation applies to: 1. Patients with MDR/RR-TB without fluoroquinolone resistance. 2. Patients without extensive TB disease or severe extrapulmonary TB. 3. 4. All individuals regardless of HIV status. 5. Children and other age groups without bacteriological confirmation of TB or resistance patterns but with a high likelihood of MDR/RR-TB based on clinical signs, symptoms, and contact history. Extensive pulmonary TB is defined as bilateral cavitary disease or extensive parenchymal damage on chest radiography. In children under 15 years, advanced disease is usually defined by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on chest radiography. Severe extrapulmonary TB includes miliary TB or TB meningitis. In children under 15 years, extrapulmonary forms other than lymphadenopathy (e.g., peripheral nodes or isolated mediastinal mass without compression) are considered severe. The rationale for this recommendation is based on evidence suggesting that the 9-month regimens are a preferred treatment option over longer regimens for eligible patients. These regimens are particularly suitable for patients not eligible for shorter 6-month regimens. Two assessments were conducted to evaluate the outcomes of the 9-month regimen with linezolid for 2 months compared to the identical regimen with ethionamide for 4 months, and to compare the 9-month regimen with linezolid to longer regimens that include bedaquiline and linezolid. Data for the 9-month regimens were primarily obtained from programmatic settings in South Africa. Adverse events were noted in 5% of participants receiving the 9-month regimen with linezolid, but no direct comparisons could be made due to a lack of data for participants receiving the ethionamide-containing regimen. The second assessment comparing the 9-month regimen to longer regimens showed lower treatment success rates (64% vs. 74%), similar rates of failure or recurrence (1% vs. 3%), and higher mortality (20% vs. 11%) in the 9-month regimen group. Adverse events were noted in 5% of participants receiving both the 9-month regimen with linezolid and the longer regimens. Based on these findings, the 9-month regimen with linezolid can be recommended as an alternative to the 9-month regimen with ethionamide, and both regimens are preferred over longer 18-month regimens for eligible patients. However, the datasets excluded patients with extensive TB disease and severe extrapulmonary TB, so the recommendation does not extend to these groups. The evidence review also considered the performance of standardized shorter regimens where injectable agents were replaced by bedaquiline, combined with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, high-dose isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and ethionamide (or prothionamide). Patients on these regimens did not receive injectable agents, cycloserine, terizidone, para-aminosalicylic acid, delamanid, or linezolid. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) judged the benefits of the 9-month regimen with linezolid to be small and the undesirable effects to be moderate compared to the ethionamide-containing regimen. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. The GDG concluded that the balance of health effects does not favor either the 9-month regimen with linezolid or the ethionamide-containing regimen. The GDG also noted that the cost of component medicines is likely similar for both regimens, as they are of the same duration and use the same medicines except for one (linezolid instead of ethionamide). The healthcare costs are also expected to be similar. However, the GDG emphasized the lack of data on the long-term consequences of neurotoxicity associated with linezolid use, which may be a concern if linezolid is used for longer periods. In conclusion, the use of either the 9-month regimen with linezolid or the 9-month regimen with ethionamide is suggested for people with pulmonary MDR/RR-TB without fluoroquinolone resistance. Both regimens are considered conditional recommendations with very low certainty of evidence.
